legal_chunks.text: SUPREME COURT OF INDIA — Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd., (2003) 5 SCC 705. Before M.B. Shah and Arun Kumar, JJ. Decided on April 17, 2003. HEADNOTE: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — Section 34(2)(b)(ii) — Public Policy of India — Patent Illegality — Indian Contract Act, 1872, Sections 73 and 74 — Liquidated Damages and Genuine Pre-Estimate of Loss. Where a contract between Oil & Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC), a public sector undertaking engaged in offshore oil exploration, and Saw Pipes Ltd. stipulated supply of casing pipes by a specified deadline and contained an explicit clause for recovery of liquidated damages at 1% of the contract price per week of delay up to a ceiling of 10%, the arbitral tribunal erred in law by refusing liquidated damages solely on the ground that ONGC failed to prove actual pecuniary loss. In contracts where it is impossible or impracticable for the court or tribunal to assess the actual quantum of compensation arising from breach, and the parties have expressly agreed upon a genuine pre-estimate of damages known to both parties at the time of executing the contract, the party complaining of breach is entitled to receive

a genuine pre-estimate of damages known to both parties at the time of executing the contract, the party complaining of breach is entitled to receive such stipulated sum as reasonable compensation without leading affirmative evidence of actual monetary loss.

JUDGMENT ANALYSIS ON SECTION 74 OF THE INDIAN CONTRACT ACT (Page 14): From the aforesaid sections and judicial authorities, the legal principles governing liquidated damages under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 can be summarized as follows: (1) Terms of the contract are required to be taken into consideration before arriving at the conclusion whether the party claiming damages is entitled to the same. (2) If the terms are clear and unambiguous stipulating the liquidated damages in case of the breach of the contract unless it is held that such estimate of damages/compensation is unreasonable or is by way of penalty, party who has committed the breach is required to pay such compensation and that is what is provided in Section 73 of the Contract Act. (3) Section 74 is to be read along with Section 73 and, therefore, in every case of breach of contract, the person aggrieved by the breach is not required to prove actual loss or damage suffered by him before he can claim a decree. The Court is competent to award reasonable compensation in case of breach even if no actual damage is proved to have been suffered in consequence of the breach

competent to award reasonable compensation in case of breach even if no actual damage is proved to have been suffered in consequence of the breach of a contract. (4) In some contracts, it would be impossible for the court to assess the compensation arising from breach and if the compensation contemplated is not by way of penalty or unreasonable, the court can award the same if it is a genuine pre-estimate by the parties as the measure of reasonable compensation.

SUPREME COURT OF INDIA — Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority & Another, (2015) 4 SCC 136. Before R.F. Nariman and Ranjan Gogoi, JJ. Decided on January 9, 2015. HEADNOTE: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 74 — Forfeiture of Earnest Money and Liquidated Damages — Requirement of Proof of Actual Loss When Loss Can Be Calculated. Appellant Kailash Nath Associates made the highest bid of Rs. 3.12 crores in a public auction conducted by the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) for a commercial plot and deposited 25% of the bid amount (Rs. 78 lakhs) as earnest money. Following prolonged extensions and administrative correspondence without proved default attributable to the bidder, DDA cancelled the allotment and forfeited the entire Rs. 78 lakhs earnest money deposit, subsequently re-auctioning the same plot for Rs. 11.78 crores—realizing a substantial windfall profit rather than any pecuniary loss. Held: DDA acted arbitrarily under Article 14 of the Constitution and in violation of Section 74 of the Contract Act by forfeiting earnest money where not only was there no breach by the appellant, but DDA suffered zero actual loss and instead made a massive gain upon re-auction.

RESTATEMENT OF LAW ON SECTION 74 & RECONCILIATION WITH ONGC v. SAW PIPES (Page 7): On a conspectus of the above authorities, the law on compensation for breach of contract under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act can be stated to be as follows: 1. Where a sum is named in a contract as a liquidated amount payable by way of damages, the party complaining of a breach can receive as reasonable compensation such liquidated amount only if it is a genuine pre-estimate of damages fixed by both parties and found to be such by the Court. 2. Inside the framework of Section 74, damage or loss is a sine qua non for the grant of compensation. The expression "whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby" means that where it is possible to prove actual damage or loss, such proof is not dispensed with. It is only in cases where damage or loss is difficult or impossible to prove that the liquidated amount named in the contract, if a genuine pre-estimate of damage or loss, can be awarded without proof of actual loss. 3. Where the authority or promisee suffers no loss

if a genuine pre-estimate of damage or loss, can be awarded without proof of actual loss. 3. Where the authority or promisee suffers no loss whatsoever (such as DDA realizing more than triple the price on re-auction), forfeiture of liquidated damages or security deposit is impermissible under Section 74.

SUPREME COURT OF INDIA (CONSTITUTION BENCH) — Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das, AIR 1963 SC 1405 : (1964) 1 SCR 515. Before B.P. Sinha, C.J., P.B. Gajendragadkar, K.N. Wanchoo, K.C. Das Gupta and J.C. Shah, JJ. HEADNOTE: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 74 — Stipulations by Way of Penalty — Forfeiture of Earnest Money vs. Part Payment of Purchase Price Under Agreement of Sale. Under an agreement for the sale of immovable leasehold property in Delhi for Rs. 1,12,500, the vendee paid Rs. 1,000 as earnest money and a further sum of Rs. 24,000 out of the sale price upon delivery of possession. The contract stipulated that if the vendee failed to register the sale deed by the fixed date, the entire sum of Rs. 25,000 (Rs. 1,000 earnest money plus Rs. 24,000 paid toward price) would stand forfeited. The Constitution Bench held that while the forfeiture of Rs. 1,000 paid strictly as earnest money was unaffected by Section 74, the stipulation for forfeiture of the subsequent Rs. 24,000 payment was manifestly a stipulation by way of penalty governed directly by Section 74.

CONSTITUTIONAL BENCH DOCTRINE ON SECTION 74 (Page 9): Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act boldly cuts the most troublesome knot in the common law doctrine of damages for breach of contract. The section eliminates the somewhat elaborate refinements made under the English common law in distinguishing between stipulations for liquidated damages and stipulations in the nature of penalty. The measure of damages in the case of breach of a stipulation by way of penalty is by Section 74 reasonable compensation not exceeding the penalty stipulated for. In assessing damages the Court has, subject to the limit of the penalty stipulated, jurisdiction to award such compensation as it deems reasonable having regard to all the circumstances of the case. Jurisdiction of the Court to award compensation in case of breach of contract is unqualified except as to the maximum stipulated; edit of reasonable compensation must be determined by the Court upon evidence of loss. The aggrieved party is not entitled to forfeit large part-payments in the absence of proof of actual loss arising from the vendee's default.

DELAWARE CORPORATE LAW DOSSIER — Piercing the Corporate Veil & Alter Ego Doctrine (Wallace v. Wood, 752 A.2d 1175; NetJets Aviation, Inc. v. LHC Communications, LLC, 537 F.3d 168). COURT OF CHANCERY OF DELAWARE & SECOND CIRCUIT APPLYING DELAWARE LAW. SUMMARY OF DOCTRINE: Persuading a Delaware court to disregard the corporate entity and pierce the corporate veil is a difficult task reserved for exceptional cases. Delaware public policy strongly respects the separate legal existence of corporations and Limited Liability Companies (LLCs) formed under the Delaware General Corporation Law (DGCL) and the Delaware LLC Act. To prevail on an alter ego or veil-piercing claim under Delaware law, a plaintiff must satisfy a rigorous two-pronged test: First, the plaintiff must demonstrate that the parent and subsidiary (or controlling member and entity) operated as a "single economic entity" such that the corporation is a mere instrumentality or sham of the owner. Second, the plaintiff must prove an "overall element of injustice, fraud, or unfairness" inherent in the defendant's use of the corporate form itself.

UNDapitalization AND THE FIVE-FACTOR SINGLE ECONOMIC ENTITY TEST (Page 4): Under Delaware precedent (Wallace v. Wood, 752 A.2d at 1184; Mason v. Network of Wilmington, Inc., 2005 WL 1653954), courts evaluate five primary evidentiary factors to determine whether an entity operates as a single economic unit or sham: (1) Whether the corporation was adequately capitalized for the corporate undertaking (undercapitalization at formation or intentional insolvency); (2) Whether the corporation was solvent at the time of the challenged transactions; (3) Whether dividends were paid, corporate records were kept, officers and directors functioned properly, and other corporate formalities were observed; (4) Whether the dominant shareholder siphoned corporate funds for personal or affiliate use; and (5) Whether, in general, the corporation simply functioned as a facade for the dominant shareholder. CRITICAL RULE ON UNDERCAPITALIZATION: Under Delaware law, undercapitalization alone is insufficient to pierce the corporate veil. Even where a subsidiary or LLC is severely undercapitalized or insolvent, a Delaware court will not pierce the corporate veil unless undercapitalization is coupled with a showing of fraud, sham, or similar injustice in the misuse of the corporate form itself (Wallace, 752 A.2d at 1184; NetJets, 537 F.3d at 177).

NEW YORK COURT OF APPEALS STATUTORY & PRECEDENT COMPILATION — N.Y. CPLR § 214-a: Statute of Limitations for Medical, Dental, and Podiatric Malpractice. STATUTORY TEXT & GENERAL RULE (CPLR § 214-a): An action for medical, dental, or podiatric malpractice in the State of New York must be commenced within two years and six months (30 months) of the act, omission, or failure complained of, or last treatment where there is continuous treatment for the same illness, injury, or condition which gave rise to the said act, omission, or failure. Unlike standard negligence actions in New York (which carry a 3-year statute of limitations under CPLR § 214), medical malpractice claims are strictly governed by the shortened 2.5-year limitations period enacted to address medical liability insurance pressures.

STATUTORY EXCEPTIONS TO THE 2.5-YEAR ACCRUAL RULE UNDER N.Y. CPLR § 214-a (Page 3): New York law recognizes three principal exceptions and tolling doctrines under CPLR § 214-a and CPLR § 208: 1. Continuous Treatment Doctrine (Borgia v. City of New York, 12 N.Y.2d 151): When a patient remains under the continuous care and treatment of the same physician or medical group for the exact condition giving rise to the alleged malpractice, the 2-year-and-6-month period does not begin to run until the date of the last related treatment. Routine diagnostic checkups do not constitute continuous treatment. 2. Foreign Object Exception: Where the action is based upon the discovery of a "foreign object" negligently left inside the patient's body during a surgical procedure (excluding chemical compounds, fixation devices, and prosthetic aids), the action may be commenced within one year of the date of such discovery or of the date of discovery of facts which would reasonably lead to such discovery, whichever is earlier. 3. Lavern's Law — Cancer Misdiagnosis Discovery Rule (CPLR § 214-a(b), enacted 2018): Where the action is based upon the alleged negligent failure to diagnose cancer or a malignant tumor, the action may be commenced within two years

Where the action is based upon the alleged negligent failure to diagnose cancer or a malignant tumor, the action may be commenced within two years and six months of when the patient knows or reasonably should have known of the negligent act or omission and knows or should have known that such negligent act caused injury, provided that no such action shall be commenced more than seven years from the act, omission, or failure.
